notes.meaning: Nehemiah begins his personal story in the citadel of Susa, the winter palace of the Persian emperor. It was the month of Chislev, late in the year, during the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes. Even though Nehemiah held an honorable position in a distant land, his thoughts remained fixed on his homeland.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Encyclopedia notes an alternative historical view placing Ezra's return after Nehemiah under King Artaxerxes II, rather than Artaxerxes I.

notes.meaning: Nehemiah's brother Hanani arrived in Susa with a group of men from Judah. Nehemiah eagerly questioned them about Jerusalem and the surviving Jewish people who had returned from exile. Even in the comfort of the palace, he cared deeply about the welfare of his fellow countrymen.

The visitors brought back terrible news. They reported that the survivors living in Judah were in deep distress and treated with contempt by surrounding nations. The stone walls protecting Jerusalem were broken down, and the city gates remained burned and useless.

Hearing about Jerusalem broke Nehemiah's heart. He sat down and wept, mourning over the city's condition for days. He then turned his grief into action by fasting, giving up food, and pouring out his heart in prayer to the God of heaven.

Nehemiah begins his prayer by praising God's majesty and power. He calls Him the awesome God who faithfully keeps His covenant, which is His sacred promise of lasting love to those who love and obey Him. Remembering God's faithfulness gave Nehemiah confidence as he brought his request.

Nehemiah asks God to listen closely to the continuous prayers he offers day and night for Israel. He openly confesses the sins of the nation instead of blaming others. He even includes himself and his family in the guilt, admitting that they all had failed God.

Nehemiah admits that the people had acted corruptly against God. They had broken the commandments, customs, and laws that God had delivered through Moses. By offering no excuses, he acknowledges that Israel's troubles were the direct result of their own disobedience.

Nehemiah asks the Lord to remember the warnings given long ago through Moses. God had cautioned that if Israel proved unfaithful, He would scatter them among foreign nations. Nehemiah recognizes that their time in exile was the exact fulfillment of God's word.

Nehemiah also reminds God of His promise to restore them if they turned back to Him in obedience. Even if they were scattered to the ends of the earth, God promised to gather them back to Jerusalem, the city chosen for His name. Nehemiah boldly bases his prayer on God's own spoken promises.

Nehemiah appeals to God's special bond with Israel, calling them the Lord's own people and servants. God had redeemed them—buying them back and setting them free—by His mighty power in the Exodus from Egypt. Because God had saved them before, Nehemiah asks Him not to abandon them now.

Nehemiah asks the Lord to hear his prayer and the prayers of all who delight to honor God's name. He asks for success and favor as he prepares to approach the Persian ruler, whom he humbly describes as merely a man in God's hands. As the royal cupbearer, Nehemiah tasted the king's wine for safety and had regular access to speak to the monarch.
